group: Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk
question:
Patient note:
A 74-year-old woman was seen in the hospital’s peri-operative evaluation suite eight days before an elective open repair of a 5.7-cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm that was discovered incidentally during work-up for vague post-prandial abdominal discomfort; the vascular team anticipates a midline laparotomy with aortic cross-clamping just below the renal arteries, insertion of a Dacron tube graft, an estimated blood loss of 600–800 mL, and transfer post-closure to the surgical intensive care unit for at least forty-eight hours of hemodynamic and pulmonary monitoring. She arrived unaccompanied by taxi, declined the elevator, and climbed one flight of stairs to reception at a measured pace without needing to pause. At home she prepares meals, gardens in raised beds for thirty minutes at a time, and can slowly ascend two residential flights while carrying a laundry basket, all without chest tightness, palpitations, or unexpected dyspnea. She sleeps flat, has not awakened gasping, and has noted no ankle swelling or sudden weight gain. Six years ago she developed sudden left-sided hemiparesis and expressive aphasia while shopping; brain MRI revealed a right middle cerebral artery territory infarct, and she received intravenous thrombolysis within the therapeutic window. Strength and language returned over subsequent weeks, and she completed outpatient speech and physical therapy; neurologic follow-up last month documented normal gait, intact cranial nerves, and only subtle word-finding difficulty when fatigued. Since that cerebrovascular event she has taken clopidogrel 75 mg daily in addition to atorvastatin 40 mg nightly and follows a low-sodium, heart-healthy diet recommended by her primary physician. Her other chronic conditions include well-controlled hypertension managed with amlodipine 5 mg each morning and lisinopril 10 mg at bedtime, stage 3 chronic kidney disease attributed to long-standing renovascular hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed eight years earlier after fasting glucose values in the 140s; lifestyle modification plus metformin extended release 1000 mg twice daily have kept her most recent hemoglobin A1c at 7.0 %, and she has never used injectable glucose-lowering therapy. She has never experienced exertional angina, has not undergone coronary angiography, stress imaging, or revascularization, and serial electrocardiograms remain free of pathologic Q waves or ischemic ST-T changes. Respiratory history is limited to mild seasonal allergic rhinitis; she has never smoked, quit social cigar use in her twenties, drinks one glass of red wine on holidays, and denies recreational drug exposure. Past operations include uncomplicated bilateral cataract extractions five years ago. Family history reveals a brother who required carotid endarterectomy at 69 and a mother who succumbed to ruptured intracranial aneurysm at 80; there is no family record of premature coronary death. Review of systems today is negative for fever, night sweats, weight loss beyond the three pounds she intentionally shed over the past month, claudication, syncope, orthostatic dizziness, abdominal pain other than dull epigastric fullness after large meals, or hematuria. After five minutes of seated rest, vital signs taken in the right arm were blood pressure 132/68 mm Hg, regular radial pulse 70 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 98 % breathing ambient air, and oral temperature 36.6 °C; body mass index is 27 kg/m². She appears well groomed and euvolemic. Jugular venous pulse is not elevated at 45°, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, and the point of maximal impulse lies in the fifth interspace, mid-clavicular line. Cardiac auscultation discloses a crisp S1 and physiologically split S2 without gallop or murmur. Lungs are clear to percussion and auscultation throughout with good diaphragmatic excursion. Abdominal examination demonstrates a palpable, expansile, non-tender mid-line mass just above the umbilicus consistent with the known aneurysm; there is no guard, rebound, or flank tenderness. Distal pulses are 2+ and symmetric in femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial distributions; no peripheral edema or skin discoloration is present. Neurologic screening reveals full orientation, fluent speech with occasional word searching, 5/5 strength in all extremities, symmetric reflexes, intact sensation, and a steady heel-to-toe gait. Pre-operative laboratories drawn one hour before the visit show hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, hematocrit 40 %, white blood cell count 6.9 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 238 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 28 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.51 mg/dL, yielding an estimated glomerular filtration rate of approximately 44 mL/min/1.73 m². Fasting plasma glucose in the same specimen measures 118 mg/dL; aspartate aminotransferase 22 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 24 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 86 U/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.0. A twelve-lead electrocardiogram obtained today shows normal sinus rhythm at 68 beats/min, PR interval 160 ms, QRS duration 90 ms, normal axis, and no ST-segment deviation when compared with a tracing from her primary-care visit six months ago. Posterior-anterior chest radiograph illustrates clear lung fields, normal cardiomediastinal contours, and a curvilinear calcified abdominal aortic silhouette. Airway assessment documents a Mallampati class II view, inter-incisor distance 4 cm, thyromental distance 6 cm, and full cervical extension. The anesthesiology plan is to continue antihypertensive and antiplatelet agents through the morning of surgery, withhold metformin on the day of operation, employ balanced general anesthesia with epidural analgesia for postoperative pain control, insert a radial arterial line and large-bore venous access prior to induction, utilize goal-directed fluid therapy mindful of baseline renal function, and conduct hourly point-of-care glucose checks while nil per os. Sequential compression devices, incentive spirometry, early ambulation with physical therapy beginning on postoperative day one, and consultation with nephrology for peri-operative medication dosing adjustments have been arranged. After a thorough discussion of potential complications—including bleeding, myocardial events, stroke, renal injury, bowel ischemia, and graft infection—the patient articulated understanding, asked pertinent questions about activity restrictions, and confirmed her intention to proceed with the scheduled aneurysm repair.

Question: What is the patient's score of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI) assigns 1 point for each of six preoperative risk factors:
- High-risk surgery: open abdominal aortic aneurysm repair is suprainguinal vascular surgery → 1.
- Ischemic heart disease: no known coronary disease, angina, or ischemic ECG findings → 0.
- History of heart failure: none reported; no orthopnea, edema, or pulmonary congestion → 0.
- Cerebrovascular disease: prior ischemic stroke counts despite neurologic recovery → 1.
- Preoperative insulin treatment: diabetes is managed with metformin, not insulin → 0.
- Serum creatinine >2.0 mg/dL: preoperative creatinine is 1.51 mg/dL → 0.
Total = 1 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 0 + 0 = 2.
Final answer: 2
